chunks: When an LDO beats a buck. The question: When can an LDO be more efficient than a buck converter?
An LDO beats a buck when the voltage drop is small, or when the load is tiny.
An LDO's efficiency is about V out over V in , so if that ratio is higher than the buck's efficiency, the LDO wins on efficiency.
It also wins when a buck's fixed overhead is bigger than the load itself.
Think of moving house. For a big load, a large truck is efficient.
For one small parcel, the truck's fixed cost (fuel just to start the engine, the driver) is far more than the cargo, and a bicycle courier is better. The buck is the truck.
Its overhead is the controller and switching losses that are there whatever the load.
The LDO line crosses the buck line at V in equals V out over c . Left of it the LDO is better, right of it the buck wins.
The region of interest is narrow: a few hundred millivolts above V out .
Dropout: the minimum gap between input and output voltage that an LDO needs to keep regulating. Break-even: the point where two options are equally efficient.
Quiescent current: the current a regulator draws just to run. Switching overhead: losses a buck pays every cycle regardless of load. Headroom: the input minus output voltage.
A buck is 90% efficient. An LDO matches that when V out over V in equals 0. 9 . For a 3. 3 volts output, that is an input of 3. 3 over 0. 9 about 3. 67 volts.
Below that input, as long as it stays above the LDO's dropout, the LDO is better. From a 3. 6 volts battery, the LDO gets 3. 3 over 3. 6 about 92 % . That is the whole idea.
"An LDO is more efficient when the voltage drop is small or the load is tiny.
Its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, so it beats a buck whenever that ratio is higher than the buck's efficiency, like 3. 6 volts down to 3. 3 at 92 percent.
At very light loads, a buck's own quiescent current and switching overhead can exceed the load, so a nano-amp-class LDO can win.
At a big drop and real current, the buck always wins."
